claims.text: Heating Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles causes thermally activated copper segregation to their surfaces.
Copper segregation initiates premelting in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Surface-segregated copper forms a liquid-like, copper-rich shell below the bulk melting point.
Copper surface enrichment reduces the local melting temperature and nucleates melting.
Copper-driven surface premelting accelerates particle coalescence.
Copper-driven surface premelting lowers the effective melting point relative to a homogeneous particle.
The initial Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are uniform random solid solutions.
Copper has a lower melting point than the relevant bulk solid solution or other principal constituents.
Copper has sufficiently low surface energy to favor its segregation to the nanoparticle surface.
The copper-rich surface layer melts before the bulk solid-solution interior.
Standard-copper nanoparticles will exhibit early surface softening and a thin liquid-like copper-rich layer during heating.
The copper-rich surface layer will thin or disappear only at higher temperatures.
Reducing copper content will delay or diminish premelting.
Reducing copper content will increase the effective melting-onset temperature.
The proposed mechanism is dominant for nanoparticles below approximately 50 nm because of their high surface-to-volume ratio.
The proposed mechanism may not govern bulk alloys or particles significantly larger than approximately 50 nm, where interior diffusion and bulk thermodynamics prevail.
Other high-entropy nanoalloys can undergo temperature-dependent phase separation involving copper enrichment at the surface.
Other high-entropy nanoalloys can reshape and coalesce during heating.
A controlled comparison of standard-copper and reduced- or substituted-copper nanoparticles can test whether copper controls premelting.
